DiffEM: Learning from Corrupted Data with Diffusion Models via Expectation Maximization

  Danial Hosseintabar   Fan Chen   Giannis Daras   danialht@mit.edu   fanchen@mit.edu   gdaras@mit.edu
  Antonio Torralba   Constantinos Daskalakis   torralba@mit.edu   costis@csail.mit.edu
Abstract

Diffusion models have emerged as powerful generative priors for high-dimensional inverse problems, yet learning them when only corrupted or noisy observations are available remains challenging. In this work, we propose a new method for training diffusion models with Expectation-Maximization (EM) from corrupted data. Our proposed method, DiffEM, utilizes conditional diffusion models to reconstruct clean data from observations in the E-step, and then uses the reconstructed data to refine the conditional diffusion model in the M-step. Theoretically, we provide monotonic convergence guarantees for the DiffEM iteration, assuming appropriate statistical conditions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on various image reconstruction tasks.

1 Introduction

Diffusion models (Song and Ermon, 2019; Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2020) have emerged as powerful tools for learning high-dimensional distributions, achieving remarkable success across a broad range of generative tasks. Their effectiveness as learned priors has led to significant advances in solving inverse problems (Kawar et al., 2021; Choi et al., 2021; Saharia et al., 2022), including image inpainting, denoising, and super-resolution. However, in many real-world scenarios, acquiring clean training data remains difficult or costly, and can raise significant concerns, as training on clean data might lead to memorization (Somepalli et al., 2023a; Carlini et al., 2023; Somepalli et al., 2023b; Shah et al., 2025), posing privacy and copyright risks. While data with mild or moderate corruption is often more readily available, particularly in domains like medical imaging (Wang et al., 2016; Zbontar et al., 2018) and compressive sensing, training diffusion models effectively using only corrupted or noisy observations presents substantial technical challenges.

The fundamental difficulty lies in the fact that standard techniques for training diffusion models are designed for settings with access to clean data from the prior distribution. When only corrupted or noisy observations are available, these techniques become inapplicable, and training diffusion models effectively reduces to learning a latent variable model from corrupted observations, a problem well-known for its theoretical and practical challenges.

Recent work (Rozet et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2024) has proposed addressing this challenge by applying the Expectation-Maximization (EM) method with diffusion models as priors. However, this approach faces a critical difficulty: in each E-step, the algorithm must sample from the posterior distribution given the corrupted observations, whereas it only has access to the score function of the diffusion prior. To overcome this, these works adopt ad hoc posterior sampling schemes that rely on various approximations of the posterior score function that explicitly incorporate the corruption process. Such approximation schemes, however, are based on implicit structural assumptions about the true prior and the corruption process, making their approximation errors difficult to quantify.

In this work, we propose a new method that combines diffusion models with the EM framework. Our key insight is that instead of learning a diffusion prior and then performing approximate sampling, we can directly model the posterior distribution using a conditional diffusion model (Saharia et al., 2022; Daras et al., 2024a). The primary advantage of our approach is its independence from specific approximate posterior sampling schemes. Notably, it can handle any corruption channel, as it makes no assumptions about the prior and corruption channel beyond requiring that the posterior score function can be expressed by the denoiser network. Furthermore, we provide theoretical analysis of the proposed EM iteration, demonstrating its convergence under appropriate conditions on the approximation error of the denoiser network. We validate our approach through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets with various types of corruption, including low-dimensional manifold learning and image reconstruction on CIFAR-10 and CelebA.

1.1 Preliminaries

Problem setup

Formally, we consider the following setup. The prior PX⋆P_{X}^{\star} is a distribution over the space 𝒳\mathcal{X} of latent variables. The forward channel (or corruption process) 𝐐(⋅|X)\mathbf{Q}(\cdot|X) maps each point X∈𝒳X\in\mathcal{X} to a distribution over the observation space 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. The observation is generated as

Y∼𝐐(⋅|X),where X∼PX⋆,\displaystyle Y\sim\mathbf{Q}(\cdot|X),\quad\text{where }X\sim P_{X}^{\star}, (1)

and we denote P⋆P^{\star} to be the joint distribution of (X,Y)(X,Y) and PY⋆P_{Y}^{\star} to be the marginal distribution of YY. This formulation encompasses classical inverse problems, which arise from a forward channel of the form 𝐐(⋅|X)=𝖭(𝒜(X),σY2𝐈)\mathbf{Q}(\cdot|X)=\mathsf{N}{\left(\mathcal{A}(X),\sigma_{Y}^{2}\mathbf{I}\right)} where 𝒜:𝒳→ℝdy\mathcal{A}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}} is a known forward operator.

In our setting, the learner only has access to a dataset {Y[1],⋯,Y[N]}\{Y^{[1]},\cdots,Y^{[N]}\} consisting of i.i.d. observations from PY⋆P_{Y}^{\star}. The forward channel 𝐐\mathbf{Q} is also known. The goal is two-fold:

  • •

    Prior reconstruction: to generate new samples from the ground-truth prior PX⋆P_{X}^{\star} approximately.

  • •

    Posterior sampling: to sample X∼P⋆(⋅|Y)X\sim P^{\star}(\cdot|Y) given an observation YY.

With this setup, the primary focus of recent work (Daras et al., 2023b; Daras et al., 2023a; Rozet et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2024; Daras et al., 2024b) has been on prior reconstruction under the linear corruption process. In such settings, the latent space is 𝒳=ℝdx\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^{{d_{x}}} (consisting of “clean images”), and there is a known distribution PAP_{A} of corruption matrices A∈ℝdy×dxA\in\mathbb{R}^{{d_{y}}\times{d_{x}}}. The observation is drawn as

Y=(A​X+ϵ,A),where ​X∼PX⋆,A∼PA,ϵ∼𝖭⁡(0,σY2​𝐈),\displaystyle Y=(AX+\epsilon,A),\quad\text{where }X\sim P_{X}^{\star},A\sim P_{A},\epsilon\sim\mathsf{N}{\left(0,\sigma_{Y}^{2}\mathbf{I}\right)}, (2)

i.e., the observation YY is a (corrupted image, corruption matrix) pair, with the image corrupted by the matrix A∼PAA\sim P_{A} and the additive Gaussian noise ϵ\epsilon. By choosing different distributions PAP_{A} for the corruption matrix, the linear corruption process (2) can model problems including random masking (Daras et al., 2023b; Rozet et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2024) and blurring (Bai et al., 2024).

Diffusion models

Given samples from a data distribution p0p_{0} over ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, diffusion models aim to learn how to generate new samples from p0p_{0}. Following Song et al. (2020), we consider the diffusion process (Xt)t∈[0,1](X_{t})_{t\in[0,1]} with X0∼p0X_{0}\sim p_{0}, and Xt|X0∼𝖭⁡(X0,σt2​𝐈)X_{t}|X_{0}\sim\mathsf{N}{\left(X_{0},\sigma_{t}^{2}\mathbf{I}\right)}. Formally, the diffusion process can be described by the following stochastic differential equation (SDE):

d​Xt=g⁡(t)​d​𝐁t,X0∼p0,\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline qn:diffusion-process}\mathrm{d}X_{t}=g(t)\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}_{t},\qquad X_{0}\sim p_{0}, (3)

where g​(t)2=d​σt2d​tg(t)^{2}=\frac{d\sigma_{t}^{2}}{dt}, and (𝐁t)t∈[0,1](\mathbf{B}_{t})_{t\in[0,1]} is the standard Brownian motion. Let pt​(x)p_{t}(x) be the density function of Xt∈ℝdX_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. It is well-known that the reverse of process (3) can be described by the following reverse-time diffusion process:

d​Xt=−g​(t)2​∇xpt​(Xt)​d​t+g⁡(t)​d​𝐁t,X1∼p1.\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline qn:diffusion-process-reverse}\mathrm{d}X_{t}=-g(t)^{2}\nabla_{x}p_{t}(X_{t})\mathrm{d}t+g(t)\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}_{t},\qquad X_{1}\sim p_{1}. (4)

With σ1\sigma_{1} being sufficiently large, we have p1≈𝖭⁡(0,σ12​𝐈)p_{1}\approx\mathsf{N}{\left(0,\sigma_{1}^{2}\mathbf{I}\right)}. The score function (x,t)↦∇x​log​pt​(x)(x,t)\mapsto\nabla_{x}\log p_{t}(x) is typically parametrized by a neural network 𝐬θ​(x,t)\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(x,t). By Tweedie’s formula, ∇x​log​pt​(x)=𝔼⁡[X0|Xt=x]−xσt2\nabla_{x}\log p_{t}(x)=\frac{\mathbb{E}[X_{0}|X_{t}=x]-x}{\sigma_{t}^{2}}, where the expectation is taken with respect to the diffusion process (3). Hence, 𝐬θ​(x,t)\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(x,t) can be learned by optimizing the score-matching loss.

1.2 Related work

Learning diffusion models with corrupted datasets

Recent advances in diffusion models (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2020) have demonstrated remarkable success in learning high-dimensional distributions. However, training diffusion models with corrupted data presents significant challenges, as most existing techniques are designed for clean datasets, and learning latent variable models is known to be theoretically and practically difficult. Several approaches have been proposed to address this challenge using diffusion models. For linear corruption Y∼𝖭⁡(A​X,σY2​𝐈)Y\sim\mathsf{N}{\left(AX,\sigma_{Y}^{2}\mathbf{I}\right)} (cf. Eq. (2)), methods such as SURE-score (Aali et al., 2023), GSURE (Kawar et al., 2023), and Ambient-Diffusion (Daras et al., 2023b; Aali et al., 2025; Daras et al., 2025) train the denoiser network using a surrogate loss function. Specializing to Gaussian corruption Y∼𝖭⁡(X,σY2​𝐈)Y\sim\mathsf{N}{\left(X,\sigma_{Y}^{2}\mathbf{I}\right)}, Daras et al. (2023a); Daras et al. (2024b) propose enforcing consistency of the diffusion model to enable generalization to unseen noise levels, while Lu et al. (2025) develop an iterative scheme to refine the diffusion prior. Recent work (Rozet et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2024) identifies the Expectation-Maximization (EM) method as a promising framework for training diffusion priors with linearly corrupted observations. However, as these EM approaches employ diffusion models as priors, they rely heavily on approximation schemes for posterior sampling (detailed discussion in Section 2.1).

Solving inverse problems with diffusion models

Diffusion models have also been shown as powerful priors for a wide range of inverse problems in computer vision and medical imaging. A line of work—including SNIPS (Kawar et al., 2021), ILVR (Choi et al., 2021), DDRM (Kawar et al., 2022), Palette (Saharia et al., 2022), and DPS (Chung et al., 2022), among others—has demonstrated the effectiveness of both unconditional and conditional diffusion models in addressing various tasks, such as super-resolution, inpainting, deblurring, and compressed sensing. As surveyed by Daras et al. (2024a), many of these approaches leverage learned diffusion priors and perform posterior sampling through approximations of the posterior score function, and the previous work on EM (Rozet et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2024) also follows this approach.

2 Expectation-Maximization Approach

For a class of parameterized latent variable models {qθ​(x,y)}θ\{q_{\theta}(x,y)\}_{\theta} where xx is the value of the latent variable and yy is that of the observable one, the Expectation-Maximization (EM) method aims to find a parameter θ\theta that maximizes the population log-likelihood of the observable variable, where qθ​(y)q_{\theta}(y) below refers to the marginal of model qθ​(x,y)q_{\theta}(x,y) with respect to the observable variable:

maxθ⁡ℒ⁡(θ):=𝔼Y∼PY⋆​log⁡qθ​(Y).\displaystyle\max_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta)\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}\log q_{\theta}(Y).

This optimization problem is equivalent to minimizing the KL divergence between PY⋆P_{Y}^{\star} and qθ​(y)q_{\theta}(y). However, direct optimization is computationally intractable for most problems. To overcome this computational challenge, each step of the EM method optimizes the following ELBO lower bound with a parameter θ^{\widehat{\theta}}:

ℒ⁡(θ)≥𝔼Y∼PY⋆​𝔼X∼qθ^​(X|Y)​log⁡qθ​(X,Y)qθ^​(X|Y).\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\theta)\geq\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}\mathbb{E}_{X\sim q_{\widehat{\theta}}(X|Y)}\log\frac{q_{\theta}(X,Y)}{q_{\widehat{\theta}}(X|Y)}.

In particular, the EM algorithm can be succinctly written as: Starting from an initial point θ(0)\theta^{(0)}, iterate

θ(k+1)=arg​maxθ⁡𝔼Y∼PY⋆​𝔼X∼qθ(k)​(X|Y)​log⁡qθ​(X,Y).\displaystyle\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}=\argmax_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}\mathbb{E}_{X\sim q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}}(X|Y)}\log q_{\theta}(X,Y).

In our setting, since the forward channel 𝐐\mathbf{Q} is known and simple, the parametrized model should satisfy qθ​(x,y)=𝐐⁡(Y=y|X=x)​qθ​(x)q_{\theta}(x,y)=\mathbf{Q}(Y=y|X=x)q_{\theta}(x). In this case, the EM iterations reduce to

θ(k+1)=arg​maxθ⁡𝔼Y∼PY⋆​𝔼X∼qθ(k)​(X|Y)​log⁡qθ​(X).\displaystyle\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}=\argmax_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}\mathbb{E}_{X\sim q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}}(X|Y)}\log q_{\theta}(X). (5)

This specialization of EM has been studied in (Aubin-Frankowski et al., 2022; Rozet et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2024), and it is also the basis of our framework. To simplify the notation, we consider the mixture posterior distribution π(k)\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)} with density π(k)​(x)=𝔼Y∼PY⋆​[qθ(k)​(x|Y)]\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}{\left[q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}}(x|Y)\right]}, which is a mixture with respect to the observation distribution PY⋆P_{Y}^{\star} of the posteriors qθ(k)​(X|Y)q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}}(X|Y)  (Rozet et al., 2024). Then, the EM update (5) can be rewritten as

θ(k+1)=arg​minθDKL(π(k)(x)∥qθ(x)),\displaystyle\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}=\argmin_{\theta}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(x)\;\|\;q_{\theta}(x)), (6)

i.e., the model qθ(k+1)q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}} minimizes the distance to the mixture posterior distribution π(k)\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}. Crucially, to implement this update, we need to be able to sample from the conditional distribution qθ(k)​(X|Y)q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}}(X|Y).

2.1 Prior approach: EM with diffusion priors

In this section, we briefly review how prior work (Rozet et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2024) performs posterior sampling with diffusion models as priors. Their methods are restricted to the linear corruption model Eq. 2, where the observation is Y=(A​X+ϵ,A)Y=(AX+\epsilon,A), where ϵ∼𝖭⁡(0,σY2​𝐈)\epsilon\sim\mathsf{N}{\left(0,\sigma_{Y}^{2}\mathbf{I}\right)} is the noise and A∼PAA\sim P_{A} is a random corruption matrix. For simplicity, to describe these results, we focus on the case where AA is fixed, i.e. the forward channel is 𝐐(⋅|X)=𝖭(AX,σY2𝐈)\mathbf{Q}(\cdot|X)=\mathsf{N}{\left(AX,\sigma_{Y}^{2}\mathbf{I}\right)}.

In the EM approach of Rozet et al. (2024); Bai et al. (2024), the latent variable models are described by diffusion models. More precisely, each θ\theta parametrizes a score function 𝐬θ​(x,t)\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(x,t), and qθ​(x)q_{\theta}(x) corresponds to the distribution of X0X_{0} obtained by running the backward diffusion process with the score function 𝐬θ\mathbf{s}_{\theta}. However, to sample from qθ​(X|Y)q_{\theta}(X|Y), one needs to approximate the conditional score function ∇x​log​qθ​(Xt=x|Y=y)\nabla_{x}\log q_{\theta}(X_{t}=x|Y=y). Following previous work on posterior sampling with diffusion priors (Chung et al., 2022, etc.), the conditional score is decomposed according to Bayes’ rule:

∇x​log​qθ​(Xt=x|Y)=∇x​log​qθ​(Y|Xt=x)+∇x​log​qθ​(Xt=x).\displaystyle\nabla_{x}\log q_{\theta}(X_{t}=x|Y)=\nabla_{x}\log q_{\theta}(Y|X_{t}=x)+\nabla_{x}\log q_{\theta}(X_{t}=x).

The second term is given by the score function 𝐬θ​(x,t)\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(x,t). To approximate the first term, Rozet et al. (2024) applies a Gaussian approximation qθ(X=⋅|Xt=x)≈𝖭(𝔼θ[X|Xt=x],𝕍θ[X|Xt=x])q_{\theta}(X=\cdot|X_{t}=x)\approx\mathsf{N}{\left(\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[X|X_{t}=x],\mathbb{V}_{\theta}[X|X_{t}=x]\right)}. Consequently, the conditional distribution of YY is approximately

qθ(Y=⋅|Xt=x)≈𝖭(A𝔼θ[X|Xt=x],σY2𝐈+A𝕍θ[X|Xt=x]A⊤).\displaystyle q_{\theta}(Y=\cdot|X_{t}=x)\approx\mathsf{N}{\left(A\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[X|X_{t}=x],\sigma_{Y}^{2}\mathbf{I}+A\mathbb{V}_{\theta}[X|X_{t}=x]A^{\top}\right)}.

Then, to calculate ∇x​log​qθ​(Y|Xt=x)\nabla_{x}\log q_{\theta}(Y|X_{t}=x), Rozet et al. (2024) introduces moment matching techniques to approximate the variance function 𝕍θ​[X|Xt=x]\mathbb{V}_{\theta}[X|X_{t}=x]. Alternatively, Bai et al. (2024) applies a simpler approximation qθ(Y=⋅|Xt=x)≈𝖭(A𝔼θ[X|Xt=x],σY2𝐈)q_{\theta}(Y=\cdot|X_{t}=x)\approx\mathsf{N}{\left(A\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[X|X_{t}=x],\sigma_{Y}^{2}\mathbf{I}\right)}.

However, these approximations all rely on the assumption that qθ(X0=⋅|Xt=x)q_{\theta}(X_{0}=\cdot|X_{t}=x) is close to a Gaussian distribution. This assumption may not hold for general diffusion priors, which are highly multi-modal. Therefore, errors in these approximation schemes can be difficult to control. Furthermore, even when the learned diffusion prior qθq_{\theta} is close to the ground truth, the posterior distribution of X|YX|Y (obtained by approximating the score ∇x​log​qθ​(Xt=x|Y)\nabla_{x}\log q_{\theta}(X_{t}=x|Y)) might not accurately represent the true conditional distribution qθ​(X|Y)q_{\theta}(X|Y) under the diffusion prior qθ​(X)q_{\theta}(X).

Additionally, the moment matching techniques of Rozet et al. (2024) are rather sophisticated and specialized to the linear corruption process. For general forward channels with non-linear transformations, calculating the score ∇x​log​qθ​(Y|Xt=x)\nabla_{x}\log q_{\theta}(Y|X_{t}=x) can be challenging even under the Gaussian approximation assumption.

2.2 Our Approach: EM with conditional diffusion model

Instead of parametrizing the prior distribution qθ​(x)q_{\theta}(x) using a diffusion model, we directly model the posterior distribution qθ​(x|y)q_{\theta}(x|y) through a conditional score function network 𝐬θ​(x,t|y)\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(x,t|y). Below, we describe the corresponding conditional diffusion process for generating posterior samples.

Conditional diffusion process

Given a latent variable model qq, we consider the diffusion process

(X0,Y)∼q,d​Xt=g⁡(t)​d​𝐁t.\displaystyle(X_{0},Y)\sim q,\qquad\mathrm{d}X_{t}=g(t)\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}_{t}. (7)

Let pp be the joint distribution of ({Xt}t∈[0,1],Y)(\left\{X_{t}\right\}_{t\in[0,1]},Y). To sample from q⁡(X0|Y)q(X_{0}|Y), we consider the following reverse-time process:

dXt=−g(t)2𝐬θ(Xt,t|Y)dt+g(t)d𝐁t,X1∼q1(⋅|Y),\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline qn:cond-diffusion-process-rev}\mathrm{d}X_{t}=-g(t)^{2}\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(X_{t},t|Y)\mathrm{d}t+g(t)\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}_{t},\qquad X_{1}\sim q_{1}(\cdot|Y), (8)

where the network 𝐬θ\mathbf{s}_{\theta} directly approximates the true conditional score function

𝐬θ​(x,t|y)≈∇x​log​p​(Xt=x|y)=𝔼[X0|Xt=x,Y=y]−xσt2,\displaystyle\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(x,t|y)\approx\nabla_{x}\log p(X_{t}=x|y)=\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[X_{0}\left|X_{t}=x,Y=y\right.\!\right]-x}{\sigma_{t}^{2}}, (9)

and the expectation is taken over the process (7) (see e.g. (Daras et al., 2024a)). For a given parameter θ\theta that parameterizes the conditional denoiser network 𝐬θ\mathbf{s}_{\theta}, we let qθ(X=⋅|Y)q_{\theta}(X=\cdot|Y) be the distribution of X0X_{0} generated by Eq. 8. In particular, when 𝐬θ​(x,t|y)=∇x​log​p​(Xt=x|y)\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(x,t|y)=\nabla_{x}\log p(X_{t}=x|y), the reverse process (8) indeed generates X0∼q(⋅|Y)X_{0}\sim q(\cdot|Y), i.e., qθ(⋅|Y)=q(⋅|Y)q_{\theta}(\cdot|Y)=q(\cdot|Y).

EM with conditional diffusion models

Based on the conditional diffusion process, we propose the EM procedure Algorithm 1, using a conditional diffusion model to learn the posterior directly.

In the E-step, the algorithm generates the dataset 𝒟X(k)={X[1],⋯,X[N]}\mathcal{D}_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}=\{X^{[1]},\cdots,X^{[N]}\} consisting of the reconstruction X[i]∼qθ(k)(⋅|Y[i])X^{[i]}\sim q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}}(\cdot|Y^{[i]}). Then, in the M-step, the algorithm uses the dataset 𝒟X(k)\mathcal{D}_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)} to train the conditional diffusion model θ(k+1)\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}, so that it learns to sample from P^(k)​(X|Y)\widehat{P}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X|Y), the posterior of P^(k)​(X,Y)\widehat{P}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X,Y) which samples X∼𝒟X(k)X\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)} and then samples Y∼𝐐(⋅|X)Y\sim\mathbf{Q}(\cdot|X). To train this model, we consider the following conditional score matching loss:

LSM,k(θ)=∫01λt𝔼X∼𝒟X(k),Y∼𝐐(⋅|X)𝔼Xt=X+σt​Z‖𝐬θ(Xt,t|Y)+Z‖2dt,\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{SM},k}(\theta)=\int_{0}^{1}\lambda_{t}\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)},Y\sim\mathbf{Q}(\cdot|X)}\mathbb{E}_{X_{t}=X+\sigma_{t}Z}\left\|\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(X_{t},t|Y)+Z\right\|^{2}\mathrm{d}t, (10)

where Z∼𝖭⁡(0,𝐈)Z\sim\mathsf{N}{\left(0,\mathbf{I}\right)} is the unit noise, and λt≥0\lambda_{t}\geq 0 is a weight sequence. It is straightforward to verify that, assuming the network 𝐬θ\mathbf{s}_{\theta} is expressive enough, the minimizer θ⋆\theta^{\star} of LSM,kL_{\mathrm{SM},k} satisfies 𝐬θ⋆​(x,t|y)=𝔼[X0|Xt=x,Y=y]−xσt2\mathbf{s}_{\theta^{\star}}(x,t|y)=\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[X_{0}\left|X_{t}=x,Y=y\right.\!\right]-x}{\sigma_{t}^{2}}, where the conditional expectation is taken with respect to the distribution sampling variables as X0∼𝒟X(k)X_{0}\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}, Y∼𝐐(⋅|X0)Y\sim\mathbf{Q}(\cdot|X_{0}), Xt∼𝖭⁡(X0,σt2​𝐈)X_{t}\sim\mathsf{N}{\left(X_{0},\sigma_{t}^{2}\mathbf{I}\right)}. Therefore, as long as the M-step is done successfully, we expect to have qθ(k+1)​(X|Y)≈P^(k)​(X|Y)q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(X|Y)\approx\widehat{P}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X|Y) (cf. Section 3).

The advantage of conditional diffusion model

Unlike approaches that rely on ad hoc approximation schemes for the posterior score function using unconditional diffusion models (Rozet et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2024), our framework directly employs a conditional diffusion model. Both the prior and the corruption channel are implicitly encoded in this model through the minimization of the conditional score matching loss (10). In experiments (Section 4), we observe that DiffEM consistently outperforms EM methods with diffusion priors. As predicted by our theoretical analysis (Section 3), this improvement is largely due to the fact that conditional models avoid the approximation bottleneck inherent in heuristic posterior sampling schemes.

Output: Posterior sampler θ(K)\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(K)} and diffusion prior θ^\widehat{\theta}

Our framework is designed to address two complementary goals: (1) posterior sampling and (2) prior reconstruction (cf. Section 1.1). The conditional diffusion model trained by DiffEM naturally serves as a posterior sampler. For prior reconstruction, we leverage the reconstructed dataset 𝒟X(K−1)\mathcal{D}_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle(K-1)} generated during the final EM iteration, and train an unconditional diffusion prior on this dataset. In particular, when the target application requires only a diffusion prior (Daras et al., 2023b; Rozet et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2024), we may directly use θ^\widehat{\theta}. In such cases, the conditional model adopted by our approach primarily serves as a means to accelerate EM convergence.

Computational efficiency of DiffEM

The computational cost of DiffEM can be decomposed as

Total Time=T𝗂𝗇𝗂𝗍+K⋅T𝖿𝗍+T𝗎,\displaystyle\text{Total Time}=T_{\sf init}+K\cdot T_{\sf ft}+T_{\sf u}, (11)

where KK is the number of EM iterations, T𝗂𝗇𝗂𝗍T_{\sf init} is the time of training a standard conditional diffusion model from scratch, T𝖿𝗍≤T𝗂𝗇𝗂𝗍T_{\sf ft}\leq T_{\sf init} is the average time of fine-tuning the conditional diffusion model for each M-step, and T𝗎T_{\sf u} is the cost of training an unconditional model to output. The cost T𝗂𝗇𝗂𝗍≥T𝖿𝗍T_{\sf init}\geq T_{\sf ft} of training diffusion model is intrinsic to diffusion-based learning methods. Thus, DiffEM can be interpreted as increasing the training cost by a multiplicative factor of KK (the number of EM iterations), which we view as the unavoidable cost of working with only corrupted data.

In general, the computational cost of EM-based methods (Rozet et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2024) can always be decomposed as Eq. 11. In our experiments, we compare the computation time KK, T𝗂𝗇𝗂𝗍T_{\sf init}, and T𝖿𝗍T_{\sf ft} of DiffEM and EM-MMPS in CIFAR-10 experiments (Table 2).

3 Monotonic Improvement Property and Convergence

In this section, we analyze the convergence properties of the EM iteration. As observed by Aubin-Frankowski et al. (2022), when the iteration (6) is exact, i.e., when the sample size is infinite and the conditional model qθ(k+1)q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}} learns the mixture posterior exactly in each M-step, the EM iteration is equivalent to mirror descent in the space of measures. Therefore, the convergence of the exact EM iteration follows immediately from the guarantees of mirror descent.

We study the DiffEM iteration, taking the score-matching error introduced by the M-step into account. For simplicity, we analyze the EM iteration with fresh corrupted samples. Specifically, we consider the variant of Algorithm 1 where, at each iteration k=0,1,⋯,K−1k=0,1,\cdots,K-1, a new dataset of corrupted observations 𝒟Y(k)={Y[1],⋯,Y[N]}∼PY⋆\mathcal{D}_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}=\left\{Y^{[1]},\cdots,Y^{[N]}\right\}\sim P_{Y}^{\star} is drawn in the E-step. We continue to refer to this procedure as DiffEM throughout this section.

Under this variant, for each kk, the reconstructed dataset 𝒟X(k)={X[1],⋯,X[N]}\mathcal{D}_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}=\{X^{[1]},\cdots,X^{[N]}\} consists of i.i.d samples from the posterior mixture distribution π(k)=𝔼Y∼PY⋆[qθ(k)(⋅|Y)]\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}=\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}[q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}}(\cdot|Y)]. We let P(k)P^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)} be the joint probability distribution of (X,Y)(X,Y) under X∼π(k),Y∼𝐐(⋅|X)X\sim\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)},Y\sim\mathbf{Q}(\cdot|X), and write PY(k)P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)} for the marginal of YY. The convergence is measured in terms of DKL(PY⋆∥PY(k))D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y}^{\star}\;\|\;P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}), the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the true observation distribution PY⋆P_{Y}^{\star} and the distribution PY(k)P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}. Intuitively, this measures how plausible the prior π(k)\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)} is by comparing the induced observation distribution PY(k)P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)} to PY⋆P_{Y}^{\star}. 11 1 Here, the convergence is not measured as the divergence between priors PX⋆P_{X}^{\star} and π(k)\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)} because in general, the problem (1) might not be identifiable, i.e., there can exist a distribution PX′≠PX⋆P_{X}^{\prime}\neq P_{X}^{\star} that induces the same observation distribution 𝐐#​PX′=PY⋆\mathbf{Q}_{\#}P_{X}^{\prime}=P_{Y}^{\star}. Therefore, convergence in terms of the priors can only be obtained under the additional assumption of identifiability (cf. Assumption 1).

Score-matching error

We define the score-matching error of the kkth M-step as

ε𝖲𝖬(k):=𝔼Y∼PY⋆DKL(qθ(k+1)(⋅|Y)∥P(k)(⋅|Y)),\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(\cdot|Y)\;\|\;P^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(\cdot|Y)),

which measures the KL divergence between the conditional diffusion model qθ(k+1)q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}} learned in the kkth M-step and the true posterior P(k)(⋅|Y)P^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(\cdot|Y). This error can be decomposed into two components: (1) the error of the learned score function, which is the statistical error of score matching (10) with a finite sample size, and (2) the sampling error, which comes from the discretized backward diffusion process (8) starting from a noisy Gaussian. When the denoiser network is sufficiently expressive, the score matching error can be upper bounded through statistical learning theory (Dou et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Wibisono et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Gatmiry et al., 2024, etc.). The sampling error is addressed by existing work on backward diffusion sampling (Chen et al., 2022; Conforti et al., 2023; Conforti et al., 2025, see e.g.,)). Therefore, under appropriate conditions, it can be shown that the score-matching error ε𝖲𝖬(k)→0\varepsilon_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}\to 0 as the sample size NN increases.

Monotonicity of EM

Our first result (shown in Section A.1) is the following approximate monotonicity property of the EM iteration in terms of the statistical error ε𝖲𝖬(k)\varepsilon_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}.

Lemma 1 (Monotonic improvement).

For any k≥0k\geq 0, it holds that

DKL(PY⋆∥PY(k+1))⏟error of prior π(k+1)≤DKL(PY⋆∥PY(k))⏟error of prior π(k)−DKL(π(k+1)∥π(k))⏟difference between priors+ε𝖲𝖬(k)⏟score-matching error of ​qθ(k+1).\displaystyle\underbrace{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y}^{\star}\;\|\;P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)})}_{\text{error of prior $\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}$}}\leq\underbrace{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y}^{\star}\;\|\;P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)})}_{\text{error of prior $\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}$}}-\underbrace{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)})}_{\text{difference between priors}}+\underbrace{\varepsilon_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}}_{\text{score-matching error of }q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}}.

Therefore, when the statistical error ε𝖲𝖬(k)→0\varepsilon_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}\to 0, the divergence DKL(PY⋆∥PY(k))D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y}^{\star}\;\|\;P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}) is monotonically decreasing. In other words, in the EM iteration, the observation distribution induced by prior π(k+1)\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)} is always closer to PY⋆P_{Y}^{\star} compared to the observation distribution induced π(k)\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}, modulo the score-matching error ε𝖲𝖬(k)\varepsilon_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}. In Section 4.1.1, we corroborate this property in experiments, showing that DiffEM can improve upon the learned prior produced by EM-MMPS (Rozet et al., 2024).

Convergence rate

Beyond monotonicity, we show that the EM iteration enjoys a convergence rate guarantee. However, this guarantee requires that the conditional model achieves small approximation error measured in the latent space. Specifically, for each k≥0k\geq 0, we define the error

ε~𝖲𝖬(k)=𝔼(X,Y)∼P⋆​[log⁡P(k)​(X|Y)qθ(k+1)​(X|Y)],\displaystyle\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}=\mathbb{E}_{(X,Y)\sim P^{\star}}\left[\log\frac{P^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X|Y)}{q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(X|Y)}\right],

which measures the closeness of the posterior likelihoods computed under P(k)P^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)} and qθ(k+1)q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}} with respect to samples (X,Y)∼P⋆(X,Y)\sim P^{\star}. The error ε~𝖲𝖬(k)\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)} can be larger than the ε𝖲𝖬(k)\varepsilon_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)} since it is measured under the unknown prior distribution PX⋆P_{X}^{\star}. Nevertheless, we show that ε~𝖲𝖬(k)\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)} can be related to ε𝖲𝖬(k)\varepsilon_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)} under appropriate assumptions (detailed in Section A.4). Below, we state the convergence guarantee of the EM iteration. The proof is in Section A.2.

Proposition 2 (Convergence of EM iteration).

For each K≥0K\geq 0, we have

mink≤KDKL(PY⋆∥PY(k))≤1K+1∑i=0KDKL(PY⋆∥PY(k))≤DKL(PX⋆∥π(0))K+1+maxk≤Kε~𝖲𝖬(k).\displaystyle\min_{k\leq K}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y}^{\star}\;\|\;P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)})\leq\frac{1}{K+1}\sum_{i=0}^{K}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y}^{\star}\;\|\;P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)})\leq\frac{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)})}{K+1}+\max_{k\leq K}\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}.

Therefore, as the number of EM iterations increases, PY(k)P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)} converges to PY⋆P_{Y}^{\star} at the rate of 1k\frac{1}{k}, up to the statistical error ε~𝖲𝖬(k)\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}. Furthermore, we can also derive the following last-iterate convergence by invoking Lemma 1:

DKL(PY⋆∥PY(K))≤DKL(PX⋆∥π(0))K+1+maxk≤Kε~𝖲𝖬(k)+∑k=0Kε𝖲𝖬(k),∀K≥0.\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y}^{\star}\;\|\;P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(K)})\leq\frac{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)})}{K+1}+\max_{k\leq K}\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}+\sum_{k=0}^{K}\varepsilon_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)},\qquad\forall K\geq 0.

Given that each EM update is computationally expensive, the above convergence rate is most relevant in the regime where DKL(PX⋆∥π(0))≲1D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)})\lesssim 1, i.e., where the initial diffusion model provides a prior that is not too far from the ground-truth PX⋆P_{X}^{\star}. Such a warm start model can be trained using existing methods (Daras et al., 2023b) that are computationally cheaper.

Stronger convergence under identifiability

Under the assumption that the latent variable problem (1) is identifiable, we show that EM achieves linear convergence in terms of DKL(PX⋆∥π(k))D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}).

Assumption 1 (Identifiability).

There exists parameter κ≥1,R≥0\kappa\geq 1,R\geq 0 such that for any distribution P⁡(x)P(x) with DKL(PX⋆∥P)≤RD_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;P)\leq R, it holds that

DKL(PX⋆∥P)≤κ⋅DKL(PY⋆∥𝐐#P),\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;P)\leq\kappa\cdot D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y}^{\star}\;\|\;\mathbf{Q}_{\#}P),

where 𝐐#​P\mathbf{Q}_{\#}P is the distribution of YY under X∼P,Y∼𝐐(⋅|X)X\sim P,Y\sim\mathbf{Q}(\cdot|X).

In other words, Assumption 1 requires that for any prior PP whose induced observation distribution 𝐐#​P\mathbf{Q}_{\#}P is close to PY⋆P_{Y}^{\star}, PP itself must be close to the true prior PX⋆P_{X}^{\star}. Intuitively, Assumption 1 quantifies the identifiability of the latent variable problem (1). We show the following in Section A.3.

Proposition 3 (Linear convergence of EM).

Suppose that Assumption 1 holds, DKL(PX⋆∥π(0))≤RD_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)})\leq R, and ε~𝖲𝖬(k)≤Rκ\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}\leq\frac{R}{\kappa} for each k≥0k\geq 0. Then it holds that

DKL(PX⋆∥π(K))≤exp(−Kκ+1)⋅DKL(PX⋆∥π(0))+(κ+1)maxkε~𝖲𝖬(k).\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(K)})\leq\exp{\left(-\frac{K}{\kappa+1}\right)}\cdot D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)})+(\kappa+1)\max_{k}\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}.

4 Experiments

We evaluate the proposed method, DiffEM, through a series of experiments. We begin with a synthetic manifold learning task (Section B.1), where we show that the conditional diffusion model yields more accurate posterior samples than existing approximate posterior sampling schemes (Rozet et al., 2024). We then conduct image reconstruction experiments on CIFAR-10 (Section 4.1) and CelebA (Section 4.2), demonstrating that DiffEM outperforms prior approaches for learning diffusion models from corrupted data.

4.1 Corrupted CIFAR-10

We next evaluate our method on the CIFAR-10 dataset (Krizhevsky, 2009), treating the 5000050000 training images as samples from the latent distribution PX⋆P_{X}^{\star}.

Masked corruption process

Following (Daras et al., 2023b; Rozet et al., 2024), we consider a linear corruption process (2) corresponding to randomly masking each pixel with probability ρ\rho, i.e., the corruption matrix A∼PAA\sim P_{A} is diagonal with entries independently drawn from Bernoulli(1−ρ)(1-\rho). In this corruption process, the observation is generated as Y=(A​X+ϵ,A)Y=(AX+\epsilon,A), with A∼PAA\sim P_{A}, X∼PX⋆X\sim P_{X}^{\star}, ϵ∼𝖭⁡(0,σY2​𝐈)\epsilon\sim\mathsf{N}{\left(0,\sigma_{Y}^{2}\mathbf{I}\right)}. In other words, each image is corrupted by (1) first randomly deleting every pixel independently with probability ρ\rho, and then (2) adding isotropic Gaussian noise with variance σY2\sigma_{Y}^{2}.

In our experiments, we set ρ=0.75\rho=0.75, σY2=10−6\sigma_{Y}^{2}=10^{-6}, i.e., each image has 75%75\% of the pixels deleted and is corrupted by negligible Gaussian noise. We also perform experiments with corruption level ρ=0.9\rho=0.9 and report the results in Table 6.

Experiment setup

Our conditional diffusion model qθ​(x|y)q_{\theta}(x|y) is parametrized by a denoiser network dθ​(xt,t,y)d_{\theta}(x_{t},t,y) with U-net architecture. We train the model for 2121 DiffEM iterations, initializing with a Gaussian prior (detailed in Appendix B). For each iteration, we train the denoiser network with conditional score matching (10) to learn the conditional mean 𝔼[X0|Xt,Y]\mathbb{E}[X_{0}|X_{t},Y]. We then compare DiffEM to prior methods (Daras et al., 2023b; Rozet et al., 2024) under the following evaluation metrics, which correspond to the posterior sampling task and prior reconstruction task (cf. Section 1.1).

Eval 1: Posterior sampling performance

The final model returned by DiffEM is a conditional diffusion model, i.e., given any corrupted observation YY, the model samples a reconstructed image X∼qθ(⋅|Y)X\sim q_{\theta}(\cdot|Y). Therefore, to evaluate the performance of posterior sampling, for each observation Y[i]Y^{[i]} in our dataset, we use the trained model to generate a reconstructed image X[i]∼qθ(⋅|Y[i])X^{[i]}\sim q_{\theta}(\cdot|Y^{[i]}) and obtain the reconstructed dataset 𝒟recon={X[1],⋯,X[50000]}\mathcal{D}_{\rm recon}=\{X^{[1]},\cdots,X^{[50000]}\} (similar to the E-step of Algorithm 1). We then evaluate the quality of 𝒟recon\mathcal{D}_{\rm recon} by computing the Inception Score (IS) (Salimans et al., 2016) and the Fréchet distance to the uncorrupted dataset in various representation spaces22 2 The Fréchet distance measures discrepancies at the distributional level. Under severe corruption (75%75\% of pixels deleted), the posterior distribution PX|Y⋆P^{\star}_{X|Y} may not concentrate around a single ground-truth. As a result, classical reconstruction metrics such as PSNR and LPIPS are less appropriate in this setting (Rozet et al., 2024). to obtain the metrics FID (Heusel et al., 2017), FDDINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2023; Stein et al., 2023), and FD∞ (Chong and Forsyth, 2020). The results are reported in Table 1.

Eval 2: Prior reconstruction performance

We also note that the models trained by existing works (Daras et al., 2023b; Rozet et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2024) are unconditional diffusion models, which can be regarded as the reconstruction of the ground-truth prior PXP_{X}. In DiffEM, the reconstructed prior is implicitly described by the conditional diffusion model qθq_{\theta}. Therefore, to evaluate the prior recovered by DiffEM, we use the reconstructed dataset 𝒟recon\mathcal{D}_{\rm recon} to train a new (unconditional) diffusion model pθuncondp_{\theta_{\rm uncond}}, which learns to sample from the prior induced by qθq_{\theta}. We then evaluate the metrics (IS, FID, FD∞, FDDINOv2) of the model pθuncondp_{\theta_{\rm uncond}} as our performance on the prior reconstruction task. We report the metrics in Table 1.

Discussion and comparison

We compare DiffEM to Ambient-Diffusion (Daras et al., 2023b)33 3 We note that the Ambient-Diffusion model was trained on a dataset with corruption level ρ′=0.6\rho^{\prime}=0.6, an easier setting than ours (ρ=0.75\rho=0.75). and EM-MMPS (Rozet et al., 2024) under the above metrics in Table 1 (higher IS and lower FID/FD scores indicate better performance). To evaluate the diffusion prior trained by these baselines, we apply their approximate posterior sampling scheme and report the metrics evaluated on the reconstructed dataset. Under all four metrics, the diffusion models trained by DiffEM outperform both Ambient-Diffusion and EM-MMPS, demonstrating the power of our pipeline.44 4 We note that Bai et al. (2024) proposed EM-Diffusion and reported FID score 21.0821.08 (corruption level ρ′=0.6\rho^{\prime}=0.6 and initialized with a diffusion prior trained on 50 clean images). However, we cannot reproduce their experiments to evaluate other metrics. Given that EM-MMPS (Rozet et al., 2024) achieves a much better FID score than EM-Diffusion (Bai et al., 2024), we believe it is sufficient to compare DiffEM to EM-MMPS. Fig. 5 shows qualitative results comparing the corrupted observations and reconstructions from our model.

We also compare the computational cost of DiffEM and EM-MMPS in Table 2, following our discussion in Section 2.2.

4.1.1 DiffEM with warm-start

Additionally, we perform experiments on the masked CIFAR-10 dataset with warm-started DiffEM. Specifically, we take the diffusion prior trained by 32 iterations of EM-MMPS (Rozet et al., 2024), and perform 10 DiffEM iterations starting from this prior. We evaluate the final posterior sampling performance and prior reconstruction quality (reported in Table 1).

The results show that using a high-quality initial prior accelerates the convergence of DiffEM: only 10 DiffEM iterations are needed. This observation is consistent with our theoretical results (Section 3). Furthermore, warm-started DiffEM outperforms DiffEM with an initial Gaussian prior in terms of the scores FDDINOv2 and FD∞, indicating that DiffEM can converge to a better distribution when starting from an informed prior.55 5 However, it is worth noting that warm-started DiffEM is computationally more expensive, as the warm-start prior requires training with 32 iterations of EM-MMPS. We also plot the evolution of the IS, FID, DINO, and FD∞ scores in Fig. 7, which corroborates the monotonic improvement property of DiffEM (Lemma 1).

4.1.2 Additional experiment: CIFAR-10 under Gaussian blur

In addition to the masked corruption experiment, we perform experiments on the blurred CIFAR-10 dataset. In the Gaussian blur model, each observation Y∼𝖭⁡(A​X,σY2)Y\sim\mathsf{N}{\left(AX,\sigma_{Y}^{2}\right)} is generated by applying a Gaussian blur kernel on XX with standard deviation σkernel\sigma_{\rm kernel} (represented by the matrix AA), and then adding isotropic Gaussian noise ϵ∼𝖭⁡(0,σY2​𝐈)\epsilon\sim\mathsf{N}{\left(0,\sigma_{Y}^{2}\mathbf{I}\right)}. In the experiment, we set σkernel=2\sigma_{\rm kernel}=2 and σY2=10−6\sigma_{Y}^{2}=10^{-6} and follow the same training procedure as in the masked CIFAR-10 experiment (details in Section B.3).

4.2 Corrupted CelebA

We perform experiments on the CelebA dataset (Liu et al., 2018), with images cropped to 64×6464\times 64 pixels following (Wang et al., 2023; Daras et al., 2023b). We consider the masked corruption process described in Section 4.1 with masking probability ρ∈{0.5,0.75}\rho\in\{0.5,0.75\} and noise level σY2=0\sigma_{Y}^{2}=0, i.e., the corruption level is moderate. We initialize the first iteration for DiffEM with the Gaussian prior (cf. Appendix B). We evaluate the diffusion models trained by DiffEM following the protocol of Section 4.1 (Table 3). As shown in Table 3, DiffEM significantly outperforms EM-MMPS. We also present sample reconstructed images in Fig. 10 and an illustration of the pipeline in Fig. 1.

Appendix A Proofs from Section 3

A.1 Proof of Lemma 1

Note that

DKL(PY⋆∥PY(k))−DKL(PY⋆∥PY(k+1))=\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y}^{\star}\;\|\;P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)})-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y}^{\star}\;\|\;P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)})= 𝔼Y∼PY⋆​log⁡PY(k+1)​(Y)PY(k)​(Y).\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}\log\frac{P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}(Y)}{P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(Y)}.

By definition and Bayes’ rule,

PY(k+1)​(y)=\displaystyle P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}(y)= ∫𝐐⁡(y|x)​π(k+1)​(x)​𝑑x=∫𝐐⁡(y|x)​π(k)​(x)⋅π(k+1)​(x)π(k)​(x)​𝑑x\displaystyle~\int\mathbf{Q}(y|x)\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}(x)\mathrm{d}x=\int\mathbf{Q}(y|x)\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(x)\cdot\frac{\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}(x)}{\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(x)}\mathrm{d}x
=\displaystyle= ∫P(k)​(x,y)⋅π(k+1)​(x)π(k)​(x)​𝑑x\displaystyle~\int P^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(x,y)\cdot\frac{\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}(x)}{\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(x)}\mathrm{d}x
=\displaystyle= ∫PY(k)​(y)⋅P(k)​(x|y)⋅π(k+1)​(x)π(k)​(x)​𝑑x\displaystyle~\int P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(y)\cdot P^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(x|y)\cdot\frac{\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}(x)}{\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(x)}\mathrm{d}x
=\displaystyle= PY(k)(y)⋅𝔼X∼qθ(k+1)(⋅|y)[P(k)​(X|y)qθ(k+1)​(X|y)⋅π(k+1)​(X)π(k)​(X)].\displaystyle~P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(y)\cdot\mathbb{E}_{X\sim q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(\cdot|y)}{\left[\frac{P^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X|y)}{q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(X|y)}\cdot\frac{\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}(X)}{\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X)}\right]}.

Therefore, by Jensen’s inequality, we have

DKL(PY⋆∥PY(k))−DKL(PY⋆∥PY(k+1))\displaystyle~D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y}^{\star}\;\|\;P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)})-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y}^{\star}\;\|\;P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)})
=\displaystyle= 𝔼Y∼PY⋆​log⁡PY(k+1)​(Y)PY(k)​(Y)\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}\log\frac{P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}(Y)}{P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(Y)}
=\displaystyle= 𝔼Y∼PY⋆log𝔼X∼qθ(k+1)(⋅|Y)[π(k)​(X|Y)qθ(k+1)​(X|Y)⋅π(k+1)​(X)π(k)​(X)]\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}\log\mathbb{E}_{X\sim q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(\cdot|Y)}{\left[\frac{\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X|Y)}{q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(X|Y)}\cdot\frac{\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}(X)}{\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X)}\right]}
≥\displaystyle\geq 𝔼Y∼PY⋆𝔼X∼qθ(k+1)(⋅|Y)[log(P(k)​(X|Y)qθ(k+1)​(X|Y)⋅π(k+1)​(X)π(k)​(X))]\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}\mathbb{E}_{X\sim q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(\cdot|Y)}{\left[\log{\left(\frac{P^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X|Y)}{q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(X|Y)}\cdot\frac{\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}(X)}{\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X)}\right)}\right]}
=\displaystyle= 𝔼Y∼PY⋆𝔼X∼qθ(k+1)(⋅|Y)logπ(k+1)​(X)π(k)​(X)−𝔼Y∼PY⋆𝔼X∼qθ(k+1)(⋅|Y)logqθ(k+1)​(X|Y)P(k)​(X|Y)\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}\mathbb{E}_{X\sim q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(\cdot|Y)}\log\frac{\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}(X)}{\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X)}-\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}\mathbb{E}_{X\sim q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(\cdot|Y)}\log\frac{q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(X|Y)}{P^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X|Y)}
=\displaystyle= DKL(π(k+1)∥π(k))−𝔼Y∼PY⋆DKL(qθ(k+1)(⋅|Y)∥P(k)(⋅|Y)).\displaystyle~D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)})-\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(\cdot|Y)\;\|\;P^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(\cdot|Y)).

Rearranging the terms completes the proof. ∎

A.2 Proof of Proposition 2

We first show that: For each k≥0k\geq 0, it holds that

DKL(PY⋆∥PY(k+1))≤DKL(PX⋆∥π(k))−DKL(PX⋆∥π(k+1))+ε~𝖲𝖬(k).\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y}^{\star}\;\|\;P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)})\leq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)})-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)})+\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}.

To simplify the presentation, we define π~(k+1)​(x)=𝔼Y∼PY⋆​P(k)​(x|Y).\widetilde{\pi}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}P^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(x|Y). Then, by definition, we have

π~(k+1)​(x)=\displaystyle\widetilde{\pi}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}(x)= 𝔼Y∼PY⋆​P(k)​(x|Y)\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}P^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(x|Y)
=\displaystyle= 𝔼Y∼PY⋆​[π(k)​(x)​𝐐​(Y|x)PY(k)​(Y)]\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}{\left[\frac{\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(x)\mathbf{Q}(Y|x)}{P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(Y)}\right]}
=\displaystyle= π(k)(x)⋅𝔼Y∼𝐐(⋅|x)[PY⋆​(Y)PY(k)​(Y)].\displaystyle~\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(x)\cdot\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim\mathbf{Q}(\cdot|x)}{\left[\frac{P_{Y}^{\star}(Y)}{P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(Y)}\right]}.

Therefore, it follows that

DKL(PX⋆∥π(k))−DKL(PX⋆∥π~(k+1))=\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)})-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\widetilde{\pi}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)})= 𝔼X∼PX⋆​log⁡π~(k+1)​(X)π(k)​(X)\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P_{X}^{\star}}\log\frac{\widetilde{\pi}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}(X)}{\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X)}
=\displaystyle= 𝔼X∼PX⋆log𝔼Y∼𝐐(⋅|x)[PY⋆​(Y)PY(k)​(Y)]\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P_{X}^{\star}}\log\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim\mathbf{Q}(\cdot|x)}{\left[\frac{P_{Y}^{\star}(Y)}{P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(Y)}\right]}
≥\displaystyle\geq 𝔼X∼PX⋆𝔼Y∼𝐐(⋅|x)[logPY⋆​(Y)PY(k)​(Y)]\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P_{X}^{\star}}\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim\mathbf{Q}(\cdot|x)}{\left[\log\frac{P_{Y}^{\star}(Y)}{P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(Y)}\right]}
=\displaystyle= 𝔼Y∼PY⋆[logPY⋆​(Y)PY(k)​(Y)]=DKL(PY⋆∥PY(k)).\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}{\left[\log\frac{P_{Y}^{\star}(Y)}{P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(Y)}\right]}=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y}^{\star}\;\|\;P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}).

Furthermore, we have

DKL(PX⋆∥π(k+1))−DKL(PX⋆∥π~(k+1))\displaystyle~D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)})-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\widetilde{\pi}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)})
=\displaystyle= 𝔼X∼PX⋆​[log⁡π~(k+1)​(X)−log⁡π(k+1)​(X)]\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P_{X}^{\star}}{\left[\log\widetilde{\pi}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}(X)-\log\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}(X)\right]}
=\displaystyle= 𝔼X∼PX⋆​[log⁡𝔼Y∼PY⋆​[P(k)​(X|Y)]−log⁡𝔼Y∼PY⋆​[qθ(k+1)​(X|Y)]]\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P_{X}^{\star}}\left[\log\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}[P^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X|Y)]-\log\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}[q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(X|Y)]\right]
≤\displaystyle\leq 𝔼(X,Y)∼PX⋆​[log⁡P(k)​(X|Y)qθ(k+1)​(X|Y)]=ε~𝖲𝖬(k).\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{(X,Y)\sim P_{X}^{\star}}\left[\log\frac{P^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X|Y)}{q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(X|Y)}\right]=\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}.

Combining the above equations, we have shown that

DKL(PY⋆∥PY(k))≤DKL(PX⋆∥π(k))−DKL(PX⋆∥π(k+1))+ε~𝖲𝖬(k).\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y}^{\star}\;\|\;P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)})\leq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)})-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)})+\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}.

This is the desired upper bound. Taking the summation over k=0,1,⋯,Kk=0,1,\cdots,K completes the proof. For the last-iterate convergence rate, we only need to use the fact that DKL(PY⋆∥PY(k))≤DKL(PY⋆∥PY(K))+∑ℓ=kKε𝖲𝖬(ℓ)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y}^{\star}\;\|\;P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)})\leq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y}^{\star}\;\|\;P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(K)})+\sum_{\ell=k}^{K}\varepsilon_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(\ell)} (by Lemma 1). ∎

A.3 Proof of Proposition 3

By Proposition 2, we have

DKL(PX⋆∥π(k+1))+DKL(PY⋆∥PY(k+1))≤DKL(PX⋆∥π(k))+ε~𝖲𝖬(k).\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)})+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y}^{\star}\;\|\;P_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)})\leq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)})+\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}.

Using Assumption 1, we know that as long as DKL(PX⋆∥π(k))≤RD_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)})\leq R, we have

(1+κ−1)DKL(PX⋆∥π(k+1))≤DKL(PX⋆∥π(k))+ε~𝖲𝖬(k).\displaystyle(1+\kappa^{-1})D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)})\leq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)})+\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}.

Denote ε~𝖲𝖬=maxk⁡ε~𝖲𝖬(k)\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}=\max_{k}\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}. Therefore, using the fact that ε~𝖲𝖬(k)≤ε~𝖲𝖬≤Rκ\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}\leq\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}\leq\frac{R}{\kappa}, we can show by induction that DKL(PX⋆∥π(k))≤RD_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)})\leq R for each k≥0k\geq 0, and hence

(1+κ−1)DKL(PX⋆∥π(k+1))≤DKL(PX⋆∥π(k))+ε~𝖲𝖬.\displaystyle(1+\kappa^{-1})D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)})\leq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)})+\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}.

Applying this inequality recursively, we obtain

DKL(PX⋆∥π(k))≤\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)})\leq κ1+κDKL(PX⋆∥π(k−1))+ε~𝖲𝖬\displaystyle~\frac{\kappa}{1+\kappa}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k-1)})+\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}
≤\displaystyle\leq (κ1+κ)2DKL(PX⋆∥π(k−2))+(κ1+κ)ε~𝖲𝖬+ε~𝖲𝖬\displaystyle~{\left(\frac{\kappa}{1+\kappa}\right)}^{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(k-2)})+{\left(\frac{\kappa}{1+\kappa}\right)}\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}+\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}
≤\displaystyle\leq ⋯\displaystyle~\cdots
≤\displaystyle\leq (κ1+κ)kDKL(PX⋆∥π(0))+∑i=0k−1(κ1+κ)k−1−iε~𝖲𝖬\displaystyle~{\left(\frac{\kappa}{1+\kappa}\right)}^{k}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)})+\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}{\left(\frac{\kappa}{1+\kappa}\right)}^{k-1-i}\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}
≤\displaystyle\leq e−k/(κ+1)DKL(PX⋆∥π(0))+(1+κ)ε~𝖲𝖬,\displaystyle~e^{-k/(\kappa+1)}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)})+(1+\kappa)\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM},

where the last inequality follows from κ1+κ=1−11+κ≤exp⁡(−11+κ)\frac{\kappa}{1+\kappa}=1-\frac{1}{1+\kappa}\leq\exp{\left(-\frac{1}{1+\kappa}\right)}. ∎

A.4 Relation between the Score-Matching errors

In this section, we provide the following upper bound for ε~𝖲𝖬(k)\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)} in terms of ε𝖲𝖬(k)\varepsilon_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}. Recall that ε~𝖲𝖬(k)\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)} is defined as

ε~𝖲𝖬(k)=𝔼(X,Y)∼P⋆​[log⁡P(k)​(X|Y)qθ(k+1)​(X|Y)],\displaystyle\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}=\mathbb{E}_{(X,Y)\sim P^{\star}}\left[\log\frac{P^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X|Y)}{q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(X|Y)}\right],
Proposition 4.

Suppose that 𝔼Y∼PY⋆Dχ2(P⋆(⋅|Y)∥qθ(k+1)(⋅|Y))≤C<+∞\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}D_{\chi^{2}}(P^{\star}(\cdot|Y)\;\|\;q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(\cdot|Y))\leq C<+\infty. Then it holds that ε~𝖲𝖬(k)≤2​(C+1)​ε𝖲𝖬(k)\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}\leq 2\sqrt{(C+1)\varepsilon_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}}.

Proof of Proposition 4.

By definition,

ε~𝖲𝖬(k)≤\displaystyle\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}\leq 𝔼(X,Y)∼PX⋆​(log⁡P(k)​(X|Y)qθ(k+1)​(X|Y))+\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{(X,Y)\sim P_{X}^{\star}}{\left(\log\frac{P^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X|Y)}{q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(X|Y)}\right)}_{+}
=\displaystyle= 𝔼Y∼PY⋆𝔼X∼PX⋆(⋅|Y)(logP(k)​(X|Y)qθ(k+1)​(X|Y))+\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P_{X}^{\star}(\cdot|Y)}{\left(\log\frac{P^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X|Y)}{q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(X|Y)}\right)}_{+}
≤\displaystyle\leq 𝔼Y∼PY⋆​(1+Dχ2(P⋆(⋅|Y)∥qθ(k+1)(⋅|Y)))⋅𝔼X∼qθ(k+1)(⋅|Y)(logP(k)​(X|Y)qθ(k+1)​(X|Y))+2\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}\sqrt{\left(1+D_{\chi^{2}}(P^{\star}(\cdot|Y)\;\|\;q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(\cdot|Y))\right)\cdot\mathbb{E}_{X\sim q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(\cdot|Y)}{\left(\log\frac{P^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X|Y)}{q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(X|Y)}\right)}_{+}^{2}}
≤\displaystyle\leq 𝔼Y∼PY⋆​(1+Dχ2(P⋆(⋅|Y)∥qθ(k+1)(⋅|Y)))⋅4DKL(qθ(k+1)(⋅|Y)∥P(k)(⋅|Y))\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{Y}^{\star}}\sqrt{\left(1+D_{\chi^{2}}(P^{\star}(\cdot|Y)\;\|\;q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(\cdot|Y))\right)\cdot 4D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_{\theta^{\scriptscriptstyle(k+1)}}(\cdot|Y)\;\|\;P^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(\cdot|Y))}
≤\displaystyle\leq 2​(C+1)​ε𝖲𝖬(k),\displaystyle~2\sqrt{(C+1)\varepsilon_{\sf SM}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}},

where we apply Lemma 5. This yields the desired upper bound. ∎

Lemma 5.

For any distributions PP and QQ, it holds that

𝔼X∼Q(logP(X)−logQ(X))+2≤4DKL(Q∥P).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}{\left(\log P(X)-\log Q(X)\right)}_{+}^{2}\leq 4D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\;\|\;P).
Proof.

Note that log⁡x≤2​(x−1)\log x\leq 2(\sqrt{x}-1) for any x≥1x\geq 1, and hence (log⁡x)+2≤4​(x−1)2(\log x)_{+}^{2}\leq 4(\sqrt{x}-1)^{2}. Applying this inequality, we have

𝔼X∼Q​(log⁡P⁡(X)−log⁡Q⁡(X))+2=\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}{\left(\log P(X)-\log Q(X)\right)}_{+}^{2}= 𝔼X∼Q​(log⁡P⁡(X)Q⁡(X))+2\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}{\left(\log\frac{P(X)}{Q(X)}\right)}_{+}^{2}
≤\displaystyle\leq 4𝔼X∼Q(P⁡(X)Q⁡(X)−1)2=8DH2(P,Q)≤4DKL(Q∥P).\displaystyle~4\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}{\left(\sqrt{\frac{P(X)}{Q(X)}}-1\right)}^{2}=8D_{\mathrm{H}}^{2}\left(P,Q\right)\leq 4D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\;\|\;P).

This is the desired upper bound. ∎

Appendix B Experiment Details

Parametrization

Following Section 2.2, we adopt the denoiser parametrization dθ​(x,t|y)d_{\theta}(x,t|y), and the conditional score function 𝐬θ\mathbf{s}_{\theta} is thus given by

𝐬θ​(x,t|y)=dθ​(x,t|y)−xσt2.\displaystyle\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(x,t|y)=\frac{d_{\theta}(x,t|y)-x}{\sigma_{t}^{2}}.

Therefore, the score-matching loss defined in (10) can be equivalently written as

LSM,k(θ)=∫01λt′𝔼X0∼𝒟(k),Y∼𝐐(⋅|X)𝔼Xt∼𝖭⁡(X0,σt2​𝐈)‖dθ(Xt,t|Y)−X0‖2dt,\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{SM},k}(\theta)=\int_{0}^{1}\lambda_{t}^{\prime}\mathbb{E}_{X_{0}\sim\mathcal{D}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)},Y\sim\mathbf{Q}(\cdot|X)}\mathbb{E}_{X_{t}\sim\mathsf{N}{\left(X_{0},\sigma_{t}^{2}\mathbf{I}\right)}}\left\|d_{\theta}(X_{t},t|Y)-X_{0}\right\|^{2}\mathrm{d}t, (12)

where λt′=λtσt2\lambda_{t}^{\prime}=\frac{\lambda_{t}}{\sigma_{t}^{2}}, and λt\lambda_{t} is the weight function from (10).

In our experiments, we adopt the following noise schedule:

σt2=exp⁡((1−t)​log⁡(σ0)+t​log⁡(σ1)),\displaystyle\sigma_{t}^{2}=\exp{\left((1-t)\log(\sigma_{0})+t\log(\sigma_{1})\right)},

where σ0<σ1\sigma_{0}<\sigma_{1} are appropriate parameters, and the scalar σt\sigma_{t} is encoded as a vector embedding. The input to the denoiser network is the concatenation of XtX_{t}, YY, and the vector embedding of the noise σt\sigma_{t}. We also choose λt=(σt2+1)⋅f⁡(t,α,β)\lambda_{t}=(\sigma_{t}^{2}+1)\cdot f(t;\alpha,\beta), where f⁡(t,α,β)f(t;\alpha,\beta) is the density function of the Beta distribution with parameters (α,β)(\alpha,\beta).

For the manifold experiment (Section B.2), we choose α=3.5,β=1.5\alpha=3.5,\beta=1.5, σ0=10−3,σ1=101\sigma_{0}=10^{-3},\sigma_{1}=10^{1}. For the remaining experiments, we set α=β=3\alpha=\beta=3, σ0=10−3,σ1=102\sigma_{0}=10^{-3},\sigma_{1}=10^{2}.

Initialization

As noted in Section 3, the convergence rate of DiffEM depends on the quality of the initial prior π(0)\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)} through the quantity DKL(PX⋆∥π(0))D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X}^{\star}\;\|\;\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}), i.e., the KL divergence between the ground-truth prior PX⋆P_{X}^{\star} and the initial prior π(0)\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}. Therefore, a better initial prior may lead to faster convergence. In our experiments, we consider the following initialization strategies:

  1. (a)

    Corrupted prior: For linear corruption processes, the observation is Y=(A​X+ϵ,A)Y=(AX+\epsilon,A). When dy=dx{d_{y}}={d_{x}}, we can consider the corrupted prior π(0)\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}, which is simply the distribution of X′=A​X+ϵX^{\prime}=AX+\epsilon. To sample from π(0)\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}, we can draw Y=(A​X+ϵ,A)∼PY⋆Y=(AX+\epsilon,A)\sim P_{Y}^{\star} and set X′=Y[0:dy]X^{\prime}=Y[0:{d_{y}}].

  2. (b)

    Gaussian prior: For general linear corruption processes, we can fit a Gaussian prior π(0)=𝖭⁡(μX,ΣX)\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}=\mathsf{N}{\left(\mu_{X},\Sigma_{X}\right)} using the observations {Y[1],⋯,Y[N]}∼PY⋆\{Y^{[1]},\cdots,Y^{[N]}\}\sim P_{Y}^{\star}.

  3. (c)

    Warm-start: More generally, we can set π(0)\pi^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)} to be any pre-trained diffusion prior as the warm-start prior. In particular, this can be the diffusion prior trained on corrupted data by existing methods [Daras et al., 2023b, Kawar et al., 2023, Rozet et al., 2024, etc.].

For the experiments (except Section 4.1.1), we adopt initialization strategy (b). Following the implementation in [Rozet et al., 2024], the Gaussian prior is fitted efficiently through a few closed-form EM iterations. An exception is the experiment on blurred CIFAR-10, where we adopt strategy (a). In Section 4.1.1, we perform experiments with strategy (c), applying DiffEM to the warm-start prior trained by EM-MMPS [Rozet et al., 2024], demonstrating that DiffEM can monotonically improve upon the initial prior.

B.1 Additional Experiment: Synthetic manifold in ℝ5\mathbb{R}^{5}

We evaluate our method’s performance on a synthetic problem introduced by [Rozet et al., 2024]. In this setting, the latent space is 𝒳=ℝ5\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^{5}, with the latent distribution PX⋆P_{X}^{\star} supported on a one-dimensional curve in ℝ5\mathbb{R}^{5}. The corruption process generates observations Y=(A​X+ϵ,A)Y=(AX+\epsilon,A) through the following steps: (1) sample a latent point X∼PX⋆X\sim P_{X}^{\star}, (2) sample a corruption matrix A∈ℝ2×5∼PAA\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 5}\sim P_{A} with rows drawn uniformly from the unit sphere 𝕊4\mathbb{S}^{4}, and (3) add Gaussian noise ϵ∼𝖭⁡(0,σY2​𝐈)\epsilon\sim\mathsf{N}{\left(0,\sigma_{Y}^{2}\mathbf{I}\right)}.

Following Rozet et al. [2024], we apply our method to a dataset of 6553665536 independent observations with noise variance σY2=10−4\sigma_{Y}^{2}=10^{-4}. Detailed experimental settings are presented in Section B.2. Figure 2 illustrates the two-dimensional marginals of the reconstructed latent distribution compared to those obtained by [Rozet et al., 2024]. The results demonstrate that our method achieves better concentration around the ground-truth curve, providing empirical evidence that the conditional diffusion model learns the posterior distribution more accurately than the approximate posterior sampling scheme of [Rozet et al., 2024] (cf. Section 2.1).

B.2 More details on the experiment in Section B.1

We implement the denoiser network dθ​(x,t|y)d_{\theta}(x,t|y) using a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). The network architecture and training hyperparameters are detailed in Table 4.

To quantify the quality of the learned distribution, we compute the Sinkhorn divergence SλS_{\lambda} Ramdas et al. [2015] with regularization parameter λ=10−3\lambda=10^{-3} after each epoch. The Sinkhorn divergence is defined as:

Sλ​(μ,ν)\displaystyle S_{\lambda}(\mu,\nu) :=Tλ​(μ,ν)−12​(Tλ​(μ,μ)+Tλ​(ν,ν))\displaystyle:=T_{\lambda}(\mu,\nu)-\frac{1}{2}(T_{\lambda}(\mu,\mu)+T_{\lambda}(\nu,\nu))
Tλ​(μ,ν)\displaystyle T_{\lambda}(\mu,\nu) :=min⁡∫(ℝd)2γ∈Π⁡(μ,ν)⁡‖y−x‖22​𝑑γ​(x,y)+2​λ​H​(γ,μ⊗ν)\displaystyle:=\min_{\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int_{(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{2}}\|y-x\|_{2}^{2}d\gamma(x,y)+2\lambda H(\gamma,\mu\otimes\nu)

We plot the evolution of Sinkhorn divergence over the iterations of DiffEM and EM-MMPS [Rozet et al., 2024] in Fig. 3. We also plot the 2D marginals of the distributions reconstructed by DiffEM and EM-MMPS in Fig. 4.

Figure 3 demonstrates that while EM-MMPS provides effective initialization when the learned distribution is far from the true prior, it plateaus quickly and fails to achieve further improvements. This is likely due to the inherent approximation error of the approximate posterior sampling scheme (MMPS). In contrast, DiffEM continues to refine the reconstructed distribution, achieving better concentration around the ground-truth curve.

B.3 Details of Masked CIFAR-10 (Section 4.1)

In this experiment, the conditional denoiser network dθd_{\theta} is a U-Net Ronneberger et al. [2015], and we adopt the same experimental setup as Rozet et al. [2024] for a fair comparison. The only major difference in the architecture arises from the fact that our model is conditional and thus for the input we need to feed two images XtX_{t} with shape (32,32,3)(32,32,3) and YY with shape (32,32,3)(32,32,3) to the model, we concatenate the images on the third dimension and thus the input shape for the model is (32,32,6)(32,32,6), the output is also (32,32,6)(32,32,6) but in the whole training process we ignore the last three channels of the output. The details of network architecture and hyperparameters are presented in Table 5.

We apply DiffEM with K=21K=21 iterations to train our conditional diffusion model and evaluate its performance for the posterior sampling task as described in Section 4.1. To evaluate the quality of the reconstructed prior, we also train an unconditional diffusion model with the same architecture on the reconstructed data. We compute the Inception Score (IS) Salimans et al. [2016] and the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) Heusel et al. [2017] using the torch-fidelity package [Obukhov et al., 2021], and FDDINOv2 [Oquab et al., 2023, Stein et al., 2023] and FD∞ [Chong and Forsyth, 2020] using the codebase from [Stein et al., 2023]. The results are presented in Table 1. We also note that the results of EM-MMPS are obtained with 32 iterations, following the original setup of Rozet et al. [2024].

As an illustration, we also plot the evolution of the IS and FID during DiffEM iterations, demonstrating that DiffEM monotonically improves the quality of the reconstructed prior, in accordance with our theoretical results (Lemma 1).

Experiments with higher corruption

In addition, we perform experiments on CIFAR-10 with corruption probability ρ=0.9\rho=0.9 (i.e., 90%90\% of the pixels are randomly deleted) and present the results in Table 6. Under such high corruptions, DiffEM also consistently outperforms EM-MMPS [Rozet et al., 2024].

B.4 DiffEM with warm-start

We plot the evolution of IS, FID, FDDINOv2 and FD∞ scores during training in Fig. 7.

B.5 Details of Blurred CIFAR-10

In the experiment on CIFAR-10 with Gaussian blur, we set σkernel=2\sigma_{\rm kernel}=2 and σY2=10−6\sigma_{Y}^{2}=10^{-6}. We apply DiffEM for K=21K=21 iterations, with the same initialization, denoiser network architecture, and hyperparameters as in the masked CIFAR-10 experiment (detailed in Table 5, Section B.3). Due to time constraints, we do not evaluate EM-MMPS [Rozet et al., 2024], as the moment-matching steps (based on the conjugate gradient method) are very time-consuming in this setting.

Qualitative study

To evaluate the quality of the trained conditional model, we sample a set of blurred images from the CIFAR-10 training set and use the trained model to generate a reconstruction for each image. We present the images in Fig. 8.

Quantitative comparison

For comparison, we use the Richardson-Lucy deblurring algorithm Richardson [1972] as a baseline, which is a widely used method for image deconvolution. We also plot the evolution of the IS and FID during DiffEM iterations in Fig. 9.

B.6 Masked CelebA

As a demonstration, we sample seven masked images from the CelebA training set under the 75%75\% corruption setting. Using the trained model, we generate reconstructions for each image after the 1st1^{\text{st}}, 2nd2^{\text{nd}}, 4th4^{\text{th}}, 8th8^{\text{th}}, and 16th16^{\text{th}} iterations. The results are shown in Fig. 10.

The denoiser architecture is detailed in Table 5. For the 50%50\% corruption setting, we trained the conditional diffusion model for 20 EM iterations, while for the 75%75\% corruption setting we trained it for 24 iterations. In both cases, we trained EM-MMPS for 9 iterations. The computational overhead of Moment Matching Posterior Sampling becomes particularly evident in this experiment, as the CelebA dataset is larger (202,599 images) and each image is higher-dimensional (64×6464\times 64) compared to CIFAR-10. We observed that each EM iteration of EM-MMPS required 4.85±0.024.85\pm 0.02 hours, whereas each iteration of DiffEM required 1.19±0.031.19\pm 0.03 hours.
